technical.reviewer: claude-opus-5 (prompt 04, full re-review). Every verdict below was re-derived from sources opened in this session: RFC 9293, 791, 768, 5737, 4291, 6056, 1035, 8446 via rfc-editor.org; refs/rfc/rfc9112.txt by grep; the repo at stage-0 (script + committed transcripts). Nothing carried over. The lab could not be started (`docker version` fails on the Docker Desktop pipe), so nc(1) behaviour rests on the committed transcript only. scope.beyond_scope is empty on purpose: the five items the ledger self-declares (203.0.113.1, ::1, exit codes/&&/||, the lab-box line, ephemeral ports) all serve reading the quoted code and output, and depth_notes (congestion control, window, keep-alive) is not touched.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9293 s2.2: "TCP provides a reliable, in-order, byte-stream service to applications." The claim's condition "while that connection lasts" is required and is present in the body and summary line 1: s3.6 says "A TCP connection may terminate in two ways: (1) the normal TCP close sequence using a FIN handshake ... and (2) an 'abort' in which one or more RST segments are sent and the connection state is immediately discarded", so bytes are promised only for the life of the connection.
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 9293 s2.2, s3.6 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293); .en.md s3, summary line 1

claim_verdicts.evidence: Nothing in the network holds it: RFC 791 s1.4 "The internet protocol treats each internet datagram as an independent entity unrelated to any other internet datagram". State at the ends: RFC 9293 s3.4.1 "A connection is defined by a pair of sockets" and "The synchronization requires each side to send its own initial sequence number and to receive a confirmation of it in acknowledgment from the remote TCP peer." The tail matches s3.6: "The user who CLOSEs may continue to RECEIVE until the TCP receiver is told that the remote peer has CLOSED also."
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 791 s1.4; RFC 9293 s3.4.1, s3.6 (rfc-editor.org); .en.md s3; quiz q1 option a

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9293 s3.5: "The 'three-way handshake' is the procedure used to establish a connection." The text around Figure 6 gives the lesson's order: "TCP Peer A begins by sending a SYN segment"; "TCP Peer B sends a SYN and acknowledges the SYN it received from TCP Peer A"; "TCP Peer A responds with an empty segment containing an ACK for TCP Peer B's SYN". s3.4.1 adds that each side must send its own initial sequence number and receive a confirmation of it.
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 9293 s3.5 (Figure 6 and following text), s3.4.1 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 791 s1.4: "The internet protocol does not provide a reliable communication facility. There are no acknowledgments either end-to-end or hop-by-hop. There is no error control for data, only a header checksum. There are no retransmissions. There is no flow control", and it "treats each internet datagram as an independent entity unrelated to any other internet datagram". Copies: RFC 768 "delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed". Loss, copies and out-of-order delivery are exactly what that leaves possible.

RFC 768: "The protocol is transaction oriented, and delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed", and "Applications requiring ordered reliable delivery of streams of data should use the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)." The header format in the same RFC carries only Source Port, Destination Port, Length and Checksum, so nothing in UDP sets a connection up beforehand.

First half holds: RFC 9293 s3.4.1/s3.5 put the initiator through the handshake on the peer's SYN-ACK, so the data waits for message 2 only. The merged half is unsupported by anything reachable: the text around Figure 6 reads line 4 as "TCP Peer A responds with an empty segment containing an ACK for TCP Peer B's SYN; and in line 5, TCP Peer A sends some data" — data in a later segment, not in message 3. s3.10.7.3, where a piggyback permission would sit, could not be read: rfc-editor's .html and .txt both truncate before it (checked twice this session).
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 9293 s3.5 Figure 6 + following text, s3.10.7.3 (unreachable) (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293); .en.md s4; quiz q5
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Your data waits for the other side's answer to the first handshake message only: your side counts the connection open the moment message 2 arrives, and message 3 needs no answer of its own, so opening a connection costs one trip out and back.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9293 s3.4.1: "A connection is defined by a pair of sockets." A socket is an address and a port, so the pair is the four numbers the lesson names, and s3.4.1 has each side sending its own initial sequence number and receiving a confirmation, i.e. holding the pair itself.

Follows from "A connection is defined by a pair of sockets" (RFC 9293 s3.4.1): two connections to the same listening port differ in the initiator's port, so their socket pairs differ. That servers do this at scale is in the local mirror, verbatim, refs/rfc/rfc9112.txt lines 1302-1305: "Most servers are designed to maintain thousands of concurrent connections, while controlling request queues to enable fair use and detect denial-of-service attacks."

RFC 9293 s2.2: "TCP reliability consists of detecting packet losses (via sequence numbers) and errors (via per-segment checksums), as well as correction via retransmission." That is the lesson's three parts — numbering, the receiver saying what it has, the sender sending again — and it places the repair on the sending side, as the body does.

RFC 768: the UDP header carries only Source Port, Destination Port, Length and Checksum — no sequence number, no acknowledgement field — and "delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed". RFC 791 s1.4 adds "There are no acknowledgments either end-to-end or hop-by-hop" and "There are no retransmissions", so nothing below UDP tells the sender either.

No allowed source documents nc(1): refs/rfc holds only rfc6265, rfc9110, rfc9111, rfc9112, and content/versions.yaml pins no netcat. The lab could not be started to read `nc -h`: `docker version` returns "open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified". The committed transcript (captured with 2>&1 by lab-run.sh) supports only the printing half: an nc line appears for the three successes, attempts 2 and 3 print nothing but the script's own echo. `-z` sending no data of its own stays unsourced.

The printed line is proven by the committed run: tcp-connect.txt line 2 is exactly "Connection to localhost (::1) 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!", the listener is the pinned Caddy (Caddyfile site ":8080"; compose service web = caddy:2.10.0 sharing the lab's network), and who-listens.txt shows ":::8080 LISTEN". The merged half is unproven: refs/ documents no nc(1) and contains neither "http-alt" nor "/etc/services"; versions.yaml pins no netcat; the lab cannot start. All that is shown is that nc prints the label.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-0: outputs/.../tcp-connect.txt line 2, outputs/.../who-listens.txt, Caddyfile, docker-compose.yml; refs/ (grep: no match)
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In the lab, `nc -z -w 3 localhost 8080` reaches Caddy and prints `Connection to localhost (::1) 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!`, in which `[tcp/http-alt]` is a name `nc` prints beside the port number and nothing the connection depends on.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9293 s3.5.2: "If the connection does not exist (CLOSED), then a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment except another reset", and s3.5.3 accepts it at the asking side: "If the receiver was in SYN-SENT state (a RST received in response to an initial SYN), the RST is acceptable if the ACK field acknowledges the SYN." So an answer, not a timer, ends the attempt. Run: who-listens.txt records "localhost:9999 is closed"; tcp-connect.txt prints "refused straight away (exit code 1)". Caveat: s3.10.7.3's state transition on that RST is truncated in both rfc-editor renderings.
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 9293 s3.5.2, s3.5.3 (rfc-editor.org); outputs/stage-0/scripts/network/tcp-connect.txt line 6; outputs/.../who-listens.txt line 5

claim_verdicts.evidence: 203.0.113.1 being reserved is proven (claim 16) and the transcript shows the attempt ending with exit code 1 and the script carrying on. Not proven, in any wording: that `-w 3` is the limit that ends the attempt and that it stops the attempt waiting for ever. No allowed source documents nc's `-w` (refs/ has no nc(1); versions.yaml pins no netcat) and the lab cannot be started (`docker version` fails on the Docker Desktop pipe), so nothing could be timed — the transcript records no timing at all. kind=behavior, so no blocker.

RFC 5737 s3: "The blocks 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET-1), 198.51.100.0/24 (TEST-NET-2), and 203.0.113.0/24 (TEST-NET-3) are provided for use in documentation", and "Addresses within the TEST-NET-1, TEST-NET-2, and TEST-NET-3 blocks SHOULD NOT appear on the public Internet and are used without any coordination with IANA or an Internet registry." 203.0.113.1 lies in TEST-NET-3.

Settled by the committed run of these exact constructs, since no allowed source documents a shell (versions.yaml pins none, refs/ holds no shell manual). `nc ... 9999 || echo "   refused straight away (exit code $?)"` printed that line with "exit code 1": the `||` branch ran because nc failed, and `$?` there held nc's own status. `nc ... 8080 && echo "   connected"` printed after a success, and no "connected" line appears anywhere a check failed. The `&&`-after-failure half rests on the same run's absence of such a line, not on a document.

RFC 4291 s2.5.3: the loopback address "may be used by a node to send an IPv6 packet to itself", and a packet with that destination "must never be sent outside of a single node and must never be forwarded by an IPv6 router". Both halves hold: ::1 names the node itself in the longer address form, and a connection reaching it never leaves the machine.

Local mirror, exact text, refs/rfc/rfc9112.txt s9 (lines 1283-1294): "HTTP messaging is independent of the underlying transport- or session-layer connection protocol(s)" and "the \"http\" URI scheme (Section 4.2.1 of [HTTP]) indicates a default connection of TCP over IP, with a default TCP port of 80, but the client might be configured to use a proxy via some other connection, port, or protocol." The hedge "as you meet it here" is exactly what that permits; s5 and summary line 5 both carry it.

RFC 8446 s1: "the only requirement from the underlying transport is a reliable, in-order data stream." TLS therefore needs the TCP connection to exist already and adds itself above it; nothing there replaces or repeats the transport's own handshake.

Refusal side: RFC 9293 s3.5.2 "If the connection does not exist (CLOSED), then a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment except another reset" — a reset is an answer, and an answer requires a reachable machine. Silence side: RFC 791 s1.4 "There are no acknowledgments either end-to-end or hop-by-hop ... There are no retransmissions", so a datagram dropped anywhere leaves the sender with nothing to read. The body stops where the claim stops.

RFC 1035 s4.2.1: "UDP is not acceptable for zone transfers, but is the recommended method for standard queries in the Internet", messages going to "server port 53 (decimal)", and "Queries sent using UDP may be lost, and hence a retransmission strategy is required." That is both halves of the claim. foundation.l1.dns precedes this lesson in the network module, so the reader has met name lookups.

The named instance is documented and the sentence states its condition instead of ranking the two: RFC 768 "Applications requiring ordered reliable delivery of streams of data should use the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)"; RFC 1035 s4.2.1 UDP "is the recommended method for standard queries in the Internet", with "a retransmission strategy is required". Neither source prices the trade-off, which is why the ledger marks it an opinion; as written it is not an unconditional recommendation.

RFC 9293 s3.6: "We have chosen to treat CLOSE in a simplex fashion", and "The user who CLOSEs may continue to RECEIVE until the TCP receiver is told that the remote peer has CLOSED also." Diagram arrows 4-5 and "the connection is closed once the other side has said the same" match that. The abort path (s3.6: one or more RST segments, state discarded) lies outside the claim's word "closing".

RFC 6056: "The IP address and port number of the client are normally left unspecified by the client application and thus are chosen automatically by the client networking stack"; "Ports chosen automatically by the networking stack are known as ephemeral ports"; the IANA range quoted there is "The Dynamic and/or Private Ports, 49152 through 65535", so the diagram's 51000 lies inside it. "Normally" is what "but few do" says, and the body's "unless a program asks for a particular one" carries the exception.
claim_verdicts.source: RFC 6056 s1, s2 (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6056); .en.md s4 and diagram

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "the port is free again for the next connection" is in no ledger entry, and it teaches the very belief section 6 refutes — that a connection occupies the listening port until it ends. A listening port is never taken: RFC 9293 s3.4.1 "A connection is defined by a pair of sockets", so the second `nc` succeeds because the listener accepts another socket pair, not because a port was released. Quiz q6 explanation d repeats the same sentence while marking option d wrong, and q2 marks option c ("only one connection is open at a time") wrong for the opposite reason.
issues.fix: s5: replace "what they show directly is that the port is free again for the next connection" with "what they show directly is that the listener takes a second connection just as readily as the first". Change the last sentence of quiz q6 explanation d (en and vi) the same way. Either add the resulting sentence to the ledger or let it rest on claim 8.
